Causal agent: High clay content + poor drainage

Recommendation: Install subsurface drainage or switch to raised-bed systems; apply gypsum at 1-2 t/ha to improve clay structure.

body:
Horizon: 5-15 years.
Where the climate is projected to shift toward drier conditions, begin introducing drought-tolerant varieties or crops now rather than waiting for the shift to complete.
Crop by crop:
- Maize: drought-tolerant maize hybrids (DT maize), or replace with sorghum in the driest years.
- Wheat: CIMMYT drought-tolerant wheat varieties, or dual-purpose barley.
- Rice: aerobic or upland rice varieties; reduce paddy area in favour of sorghum or cowpea.
- Potato: move potato to cooler and wetter seasons only; introduce sweet potato as a dry-season alternative.
- Beans: cowpea or tepary bean, which tolerate 30% less rainfall than common bean.
- Coffee: shade-grown Robusta or Liberica; Arabica will face severe heat stress.
- Banana: plantain varieties with higher drought tolerance; reduce overall area.
- Any other crop: explore sorghum, millet, cowpea or cassava as more resilient alternatives.

Applies when: climate_shift_direction == aridification.

Horizon: now.
Building soil water storage is the single highest-return investment for drought resilience. Every 1% increase in soil organic matter adds about 20,000 L/ha of water holding capacity.
Apply compost at 3-5 t/ha annually, retain all crop residues, and introduce a legume cover crop in the off-season.
Soil texture sets the starting point: a soil above about 55% sand holds limited water, loam and clay soils hold moderate amounts.

Applies when: climate_shift_direction == aridification.

Horizon: 5-15 years.
A projected shift toward wetter conditions means fungal and bacterial disease pressure will increase significantly.
Invest in field drainage now - raised beds or ridge-furrow systems. Select disease-resistant varieties.
Crop by crop:
- Maize: grey leaf spot and northern blight will become more frequent.
- Wheat: Fusarium head blight and septoria are the primary risks.
- Potato: late blight pressure will intensify - resistant varieties are critical.
- Coffee: coffee leaf rust will spread to higher altitudes.
- Banana: black Sigatoka will require more frequent fungicide cycles.
- Any other crop: scout regularly for new fungal and bacterial diseases.

Applies when: climate_shift_direction == moistening.

Horizon: now, urgent.
Soil organic carbon below 8 g/kg gives a soil almost no buffer against climate extremes. Under any climate trajectory, low SOC means faster moisture loss, weaker nutrient cycling and lower yield stability.
Target 15+ g/kg SOC through compost, cover crops and minimum tillage. This is the most cost-effective climate adaptation available.

Applies when: soc_g_kg < 8 g/kg; climate_shifting == True.

Soil organic carbon below 8 g/kg gives a soil almost no buffer against climate extremes. Under any climate trajectory, low SOC means faster moisture loss, weaker nutrient cycling and lower yield stability.
Target 15+ g/kg SOC through compost, cover crops and minimum tillage. This is the most cost-effective climate adaptation available.

body:
A candidate crop is scored against the ideal conditions recorded for it in the disease library, weighted as follows: temperature fit 2 points, rainfall fit 2 points, soil pH fit 2 points, humidity fit 1 point, drainage fit 1 point. The score is the points earned as a percentage of the points available.
Temperature outside the crop's ideal band costs a further 1.5 points, in either direction.
Rainfall is scored against a window from 0.45 to 1.9 times the crop's ideal weekly rainfall; below the bottom of that window the crop needs irrigation.
Drainage scoring: a crop wanting flooded conditions scores fully on poorly drained soil; a crop wanting well-drained soil scores fully on well-drained soil and about 60% on moderately drained soil.
Candidates below 40% are dropped outright; where the climate is not shifting the bar rises to 70%.

body:
Priority: high below pH 5.0, medium between pH 5.0 and 5.5.
A soil pH below 5.5 is under the optimal range (6.0-7.0) for most crops. At this pH, phosphorus, calcium and magnesium availability is reduced, and aluminium and manganese toxicity become risks.
Apply agricultural lime at 1-3 t/ha depending on buffer pH. Re-test the soil after 6 months.
Crop sensitivity to acidity:
- Maize is moderately sensitive to acidity - yields drop significantly below pH 5.5.
- Wheat is sensitive to aluminium toxicity at low pH; performance will be poor below 5.5.
- Soybean rhizobium nitrogen fixation fails below pH 5.8; it is critical to lime before planting.
- Potato tolerates mild acidity but scab risk increases above pH 5.5 - lime with caution.
- Common beans are highly sensitive to acidity; liming is strongly recommended.
- Flooded rice is more tolerant of acidity than upland crops; monitor, but less urgent.
- Any other crop may experience reduced nutrient uptake at this pH.

Applies when: ph < 5.5 pH.

Priority: medium.
Sandy soil with a cation exchange capacity below 10 mmol/kg cannot hold nutrients effectively. Standard broadcast fertilizer applications will result in significant leaching, especially of nitrogen and potassium.
Split all fertilizer applications into 3-4 smaller doses through the season. Fertigation (fertilizer through the irrigation water) is ideal for this soil type. Consider polymer-coated slow-release fertilizers.

Used for: Cropland extent and field context (is-this-cropland / land cover / irrigated-vs-rainfed / crop type / field polygon)
Bands: classification, confidence
Units: classification = 0 or 100 (binary, NOT a percentage); confidence = 0-100 integer percent
Scaling CropUp applies: NO scaling on classification: it is literally 0 or 100 and means absent/present. Divide confidence by 100 to get a 0-1 probability. Verified against the EE STAC description: 'Each product (image) has a binary classification (0 or 100) and a confidence (0-100) band.'
Coverage: Global, but tiled into 106 agro-ecological zones (AEZ); a point can fall inside TWO overlapping AEZ tiles (Salinas falls in aez_id 6137 AND 37176). Products are masked outside cropland, so maize/irrigation return null on non-crop pixels even where the tile exists.
Native resolution: 10 m
Temporal range: 2021 (nominal), system:time_start 2020-11-18
Licence: CC-BY-4.0 (from EE STAC 'license' field)
Notes: THE single most valuable asset in this family and the only one that answers all three questions (cropland / crop type / irrigation) globally at 10 m. How to query a point: ic.filterBounds(pt).filter(ee.Filter.eq('product', P)).qualityMosaic('confidence') — qualityMosaic is required, not optional, because of the overlapping-AEZ duplication. product is one of {temporarycrops(106 imgs), irrigation(225), maize(133), wintercereals(106), springcereals(21)}; season is one of {tc-annual, tc-maize-main, tc-maize-second, tc-wintercereals, tc-springcereals}. aez_id has 106 distinct values. - Salinas, United States: temporarycrops: classification=0, confidence=99 -> NOT cropland. All other products masked (null). At a true Salinas Valley field (36.46,-121.41): temporarycrops=100 conf 48, irrigation=100 conf 45 -> IRRIGATED.

Earth Engine asset: projects/sat-io/open-datasets/global_fertilizer_use_centroid (FeatureCollection (7529 point features = country centroid x crop x report))
Used for: Farm inputs and practices (fertilizer, pesticide, tillage)
Bands: Country, ISO3_code, Crop, Year, Crop_area_k_ha, N_rate_kg_ha, P2O5_rate_kg_ha, K2O_rate_kg_ha, N_pc_fert, P2O5_pc_fert, K2O_pc_fert, Aver_N_rate_kg_ha, Aver_P2O5_rate_kg_ha, Aver_K2O_rate_kg_ha, N_k_t, P2O5_k_t, K2O_k_t, FUBC_report_number, Year_FUBC_publication, Region_IFA
Units: kg nutrient/ha/yr for the *_rate and Aver_*_rate columns; percent for *_pc_fert; kilo-tonnes for *_k_t; kilo-hectares for Crop_area_k_ha
Scaling CropUp applies: NONE numerically, BUT every attribute is stored as a STRING with literal 'NA' for missing - you must cast to float and treat 'NA' as null. Geometry is a country CENTROID point, so a spatial filterBounds on a farm location returns nothing; you must join by country name (I used USDOS/LSIB_SIMPLE/2017 'country_na', which matches FUBC 'Country' exactly for both 'Tanzania' and 'United States').
Coverage: 111 countries incl. Tanzania (43 rows) and United States. Tanzania crops available: Cassava, Coffee, Coffee green, Cotton, Maize, Millet, Other cereals, Potato-sweet, Pulses, Residual, Rice, Roots/tubers, Sorghum, Sugar cane, Tea, Tobacco, Vegetables, Wheat.
Temporal range: Tanzania rows: 1990, 1992, 1992/93, 1997, 2016. United States rows: 1992/93, 1994, 1996, 1998, 2006, 2007, 2010, 2014, 2019. Note the 2006-2014 US rows are entirely NA.
Licence: CC0-1.0 (public domain dedication)
Notes: THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT DATASET FOR THE FERTILIZER QUESTIONS, because it is the only source that carries the distinction that keeps the advice safe. I pulled the authoritative column metadata from the authors' own repo (raw.githubusercontent.com/ludemannc/FUBC_1_to_9_2022/main/results/Meta_data_FUBC_1_to_9_data.csv) rather than guessing. Verbatim: N_rate_kg_ha = 'Mean application rate of nitrogen to area of crop that actually received fertilizer (see N_pc_fert for percentage of crop area where N was applied)'. Aver_N_rate_kg_ha = 'Mean application rate of nitrogen across total crop area'. N_pc_fert = 'Percentage of total crop area that received any nitrogen fertilizer'. So for Tanzanian maize the two numbers are 120 kg N/ha (what a farmer who fertilizes actually puts on, 1990) versus ~16.5-17.8 kg N/ha (the national area-average, because only 10-15% of maize land gets anything). 120 x 0.15 = 18, which is essentially exactly the NPKGRIDS raster value of 17.83 - that arithmetic agreement is the proof that the NPKGRIDS grid maps the AREA-AVERAGE concept, not a dose. In the US the gap nearly vanishes (97-100% of maize area fertilized, so 150 on-fertilized vs 157.6 across-total), which is why this trap is invisible if you only test on US data. CAVEAT: the newest Tanzania maize row is 2016 and the on-fertilized-area rates are from 1990-1997, i.e. ~30 years old.
Readings observed at the three verification points when this registry was built (they verify the asset, they are not a measurement of your field):
- Arusha, Tanzania: Tanzania Maize. 1990: rate-on-fertilized-area N=120, P2O5=60, K2O=45 with only 15% of maize area fertilized. 1992/93, 1992, 1992 (reports 2,3,4): N=80, P2O5=40, K2O=1 at 10% of area. 1997: N=80, P2O5=40, K2O=5 at 10%. 2016 (FUBC 9, published 2022): rate-across-TOTAL-area N=16.5466, P2O5=2.6217, K2O=0.0. Tanzania Rice 1990: N=50, P2O5=0, K2O=0; 1992-1997: N=40, P2O5=20.
- Morogoro, Tanzania: Identical to Arusha - this is a national table, there is no sub-national resolution for Tanzania.
- Salinas, United States: United States Maize. 1992/93: N=138, P2O5=63, K2O=89 at 97% of area fertilized. 1994: N=144 at 97%. 1996: N=148.9 at 96%. 1998: N=150, P2O5=70, K2O=90 at 100%. 2019 (FUBC 9): rate-across-total-area N=157.6476, P2O5=54.0138, K2O=58.2842.

Scaling CropUp applies: NONE - float, already kg ai/ha/yr. BUT there are NEGATIVE SENTINELS that a naive read reports as a real rate. I counted them on the global grid for Corn/Glyphosate/2020/HIGH: exactly -2 on 1,041,381 px, exactly -1.5 on 310,592 px, exactly -1 on 241 px, plus 19,986 px of sparse small negatives in (-1, -0.001) which are model noise and should be clamped to 0 (valid px >= 0: 114,609). Global range is -2 to 6.74. The catalog page documents none of this. Filter anything <= -0.999 as no-data.
Coverage: Global, 5 arc-min. Returns real values at Arusha and Morogoro for Corn; returns ONLY sentinels for Corn at Salinas. 10 crop classes: 6 dominant (Corn, Soybean, Wheat, Cotton, Rice, Alfalfa) + 4 aggregated (VegFru, OrcGra, PasHay, Other). NOTE maize = 'Corn'. No cassava, sorghum, millet, banana, coffee, or bean class - most Tanzanian staples fall into the catch-all 'Other'.
Native resolution: 5 arc-min (~10 km), 4306x1681, WGS84, origin -178.9167/84.0408

Notes: PROPERTY NAMES: the catalog docs page CONTRADICTS ITSELF. Its prose says properties are 'active_ingredient' and 'estimate_type'; the actual asset properties (verified via getInfo) are 'ingredient' (title-case, e.g. 'Glyphosate'), 'ingredient_normalized' (lowercase), 'year' (INTEGER not string), 'estimate' ('HIGH'/'LOW'), 'crop', 'crop_type', 'pesticide_class'. The JS snippet on the same page is the correct one. Use ingredient/estimate/year. Sanity check passed: Iowa Corn glyphosate = 1.310 and Illinois = 1.259 kg ai/ha/yr, which matches the real-world 0.8-2.2 kg ai/ha band, and the Salinas VegFru fumigant profile (metam potassium / 1,3-D / metam / chloropicrin) is exactly the real Salinas strawberry fumigant signature. So the values are being read correctly; the Tanzania values really are ~1e-5, i.e. the model says essentially no pesticide on Tanzanian maize.

- Arusha, Tanzania: Corn 2020 HIGH: Glyphosate 1.279e-05, Atrazine 4.970e-06, Acetochlor 2.484e-06, Metolachlor(-s) 2.111e-06, 2,4-d 8.287e-07, Paraquat 3.851e-07, Chlorpyrifos 2.072e-09 kg ai/ha/yr. All effectively zero.
- Morogoro, Tanzania: Corn 2020 HIGH: Glyphosate 1.353e-05, Atrazine 4.560e-06, Acetochlor 2.303e-06, Metolachlor(-s) 1.851e-06, 2,4-d 8.918e-07, Paraquat 3.885e-07, Chlorpyrifos 1.881e-09. Rice 2020 HIGH: Propanil 2.439e-05. All effectively zero.

body:
Earth Engine asset: projects/sat-io/open-datasets/PEST-CHEMGRIDS/quality_index (ImageCollection (200 images = 10 crops x 20 ingredients))
Used for: Farm inputs and practices (fertilizer, pesticide, tillage)
Bands: quality_index
Units: dimensionless, 0-1 (higher = better)
Scaling CropUp applies: NONE - float 0-1. Sentinel: global min is -1, and 0 marks invalid pixels (0 co-occurs exactly with the -1.5 application-rate sentinel). Treat <= -0.999 as no-data and 0 as 'no estimate here'.
Coverage: Global, same 5 arc-min grid as application_rates. One image per crop-ingredient pair, time-independent.
Native resolution: 5 arc-min (~10 km), identical grid to application_rates
Temporal range: Time-independent (single layer per crop-ingredient, applies to all three year layers)
Licence: CC-BY-4.0
Notes: CRITICAL AND COUNTERINTUITIVE: the quality index is very nearly a GLOBAL CONSTANT per crop-ingredient, NOT a local confidence. For Corn/Glyphosate I sampled Iowa, Illinois, Arusha, Morogoro and Nairobi and got the byte-identical value 0.7568864822387695 at all five; Netherlands 0.7930; Salinas and Brazil 0 (invalid). For VegFru the value is identical at Arusha, Morogoro and Salinas. So a QI of 0.76 at Arusha does NOT mean the Tanzanian estimate is trustworthy - it is a global model-fit score for that crop-chemical combination, dominated by the USGS US survey data the model was trained on. Presenting it to a farmer as 'data confidence: 76%' would be actively misleading. Use it only to RANK chemicals or to suppress a layer entirely, never as a local reliability score.
Readings observed at the three verification points when this registry was built (they verify the asset, they are not a measurement of your field):
- Arusha, Tanzania: Corn: Glyphosate 0.7569, Acetochlor 0.7979, Atrazine 0.7282, Metolachlor(-s) 0.7129, 2,4-d 0.7131, Paraquat 0.6777, Chlorpyrifos 0.6404. Across all 20 Corn ingredients: min 0.524, max 0.798, mean 0.673.
- Morogoro, Tanzania: Identical to Arusha for every ingredient (min 0.524, max 0.798, mean 0.673).
- Salinas, United States: Corn: 0 for every ingredient (matches the -1.5 rate sentinel = no estimate). VegFru: Metam 0.5265, Dichloropropene 0.5502, Chlorothalonil 0.5482, Glyphosate 0.6365, Chloropicrin 0.4977.

Earth Engine asset: projects/sat-io/open-datasets/global_tillage_production (FeatureCollection (4403 point features))
Used for: Farm inputs and practices (fertilizer, pesticide, tillage)
Bands: crop, site_country, location, harvest_year, sowing_year, yield_ct, yield_nt, rel_yl_chg, yrs_from_nt, init_yr_nt, n_inp, ST, pH_surface_layer, Tave, Tmin, Tmax, P, PB, E, soil_cover_ct, soil_cover_nt, rm_ct, rm_nt, author, journal, year, other
Units: yield_ct / yield_nt in kg/ha (conventional-till and no-till yields); rel_yl_chg is a dimensionless fraction (no-till relative to conventional-till, so -0.66 = no-till yielded 66% less); Tave/Tmin/Tmax in degC; P in mm
Scaling CropUp applies: NONE - numeric attributes are already real floats (unlike the FUBC table, these are not strings). Geometry is the trial site point.
Coverage: 50 countries. Heavily skewed to USA (1692), Canada (565), India (404), China (395), Spain (154), Brazil (100). Africa is thin: South Africa 74, Ethiopia 51, Nigeria 40, Kenya 39, Malawi 38, Rwanda 32, Zimbabwe 29, Burkina Faso 14, Cameroon 4, Ghana 2, Algeria 2, Morocco 4, and TANZANIA ONLY 3. Crops: maize 1690, wheat.winter 1041, soybean 583, barley.spring 232, wheat.spring 209, rice 195, sorghum 160, barley.winter 138, cotton 94, sunflower 61.
Native resolution: Point locations, not gridded. Not a raster and not interpolatable.
Temporal range: Individual trials, roughly 1980s-2010s. Tanzania's three trials have harvest_year 1997, 1997 and 2000.

Notes: MISLABELLED BY EXPECTATION. This is NOT a map of what tillage farmers use - it is a meta-analysis database of published paired field experiments comparing no-till against conventional till. For CropUp its honest use is narrow: if a Tanzanian farmer asks about conservation agriculture / no-till, you can say that in 39 East African maize trials the median outcome was a 6% yield LOSS and no-till won in only about a third of them, and that the three Tanzanian trials on record are sorghum at Dodoma where two of three lost 62-66% of yield. That is a genuinely useful, genuinely cautionary answer, and it is the opposite of the usual no-till marketing. Note the trials mostly report early years after conversion (yrs_from_nt = 2 for the Kenyan set, 1-4 for Tanzania), and no-till is known to need several years before benefits appear - say so.
Readings observed at the three verification points when this registry was built (they verify the asset, they are not a measurement of your field):

- Morogoro, Tanzania: Only 3 trials within 500 km and ZERO of them are maize - all three are SORGHUM at Dodoma (-5.17, 35.73), Kabanza & Rwehumbiza 2007. Values: 1997 CT 1490 / NT 510 kg/ha (-0.658); 1997 CT 1100 / NT 1250 (+0.136); 2000 CT 1690 / NT 640 (-0.621).
- Salinas, United States: ZERO trials within 500 km. The 1692 US trials are Midwest and Great Plains, none in coastal California.

Used for: Water, evapotranspiration and irrigation signals

Units: evaporation and precipitation in METRES; volumetric_soil_water in m3/m3
Scaling CropUp applies: CRITICAL: evaporation/precipitation are stored in METRES, and evaporation is NEGATIVE for an upward (evaporative) flux. mm = value * -1000 for evaporation, value * 1000 for precipitation. Soil water layers need no scaling.
Coverage: GLOBAL
Native resolution: 11132 m
Temporal range: 1950-01-02 -> 2026-09-06; 10 days stale
Licence: Copernicus / CC-BY-4.0-like
Notes: THE BIGGEST SCALING/INTERPRETATION TRAP IN THIS FAMILY, and I nearly shipped it wrong. ERA5-Land 'potential_evaporation' is NOT FAO-56 reference ET - it is ECMWF's own open-water-style potential evaporation. Measured against the FAO-56 normals it runs ~1.5-1.9x too high (Arusha 9.1 vs 4.7, Morogoro 7.3 vs 4.9, Salinas 7.1 vs 6.5 mm/day), and TerraClimate's ASCE Penman-Monteith PET for the same month agrees with FAO-56, not with ERA5 (Arusha 4.08, Morogoro 4.51, Salinas 4.75 mm/day). My first draft of get_water_status used it as the ETo denominator and reported a stress ratio of 0.175 at Arusha - i.e. it made a normally-watered field look severely stressed. Single days are also very noisy (Morogoro 15.1 vs a 7.3 mm/day 10-day mean), so always average. Its total_evaporation IS useful: 1.63 mm/day at Arusha independently corroborates SSEBop's 1.95 mm/day.

Units: categorical integer class code. Observed range over Africa for the 47 normal crops: 0..12 (plus -1 = nodata). Only the anomalous 'rapeseed' band reaches 13.
Scaling CropUp applies: NONE — integer class code.
Coverage: Africa only. Masked at the exact Arusha pixel (same mask as crop_suitability).
Native resolution: 30 arcsec / 927.66 m
Temporal range: 1991-2010
Licence: CC BY 4.0
Notes: NO CLASS TABLE IS PUBLISHED anywhere (not in the catalog docs page, not in the GMD paper, not in the asset properties). I DERIVED it from the CropSuite v1.0 source (github.com/flozabel/CropSuite tag v1.0, src/crop_suitability_main.py writes limiting_factor.inf with codes 0-3 hard-coded and codes 4+ = the config parameter list in order) and then CROSS-VALIDATED it against SoilGrids and SRTM in EE. TABLE: -1 nodata | 0 temperature | 1 precipitation | 2 climate variability (crop-failure recurrence) | 3 photoperiod | 4 soil base saturation | 5 coarse fragments | 6 soil pH | 7 salinity (EC) | 8 soil texture | 9 soil organic carbon | 10 sodicity (ESP) | 11 soil depth | 12 slope. EVIDENCE: (a) code 1 covers 100% of the Sahara under rainfed and 0% under irrigated — precipitation, certain; (b) code 6 pixels (maize, n=348k at 5 km) have 75% of pixels with SoilGrids pH outside 5.5-7.8 and mean maize pH-membership 37 vs 60 Africa-wide, and code 6 covers 87% of the Congo Basin where the GMD paper explicitly says maize is pH-limited — pH, strong; (c) code 9 pixels have SoilGrids SOC 0.57% vs 1.12% Africa mean, lowest of any class — organic carbon, strong; (d) code 8 for rice has sand 59.1% vs 51.8% mean and for cassava 72.6% — texture, strong; (e) code 12 pixels in the East African highlands have mean SRTM slope 5.87 deg vs 1.68 deg regional — slope, strong; (f) code 11 pixels have the highest coarse-fragment volume (26.0% vs 14.2% mean) — soil depth / rocky, moderate. CONFIDENCE: codes 0-3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12 are well supported; codes 4, 5, 7, 10 follow the source ordering but I could not independently confirm them (base saturation and sodicity are not in SoilGrids, and code 7 essentially never occurs). Treat 4/5/7/10 as 'a soil chemical constraint' if precision matters.
